title: Tech Blog Radar Weekly
description: Weekly digest of trending tech blog articles

top_articles.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: The Developer Guide
top_articles.summary: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-source multimodal embedding model that maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space. Developers can use the sentence-transformers library to selectively load modular modality encoders—ranging from 270M to 740M parameters—to optimize memory usage. Additionally, Matryoshka Representation Learning enables dynamic dimension truncation down to 128d, significantly reducing vector database storage requirements while maintaining high retrieval performance.

top_articles.title: Announcing DPoP Support for Google OAuth: Securing Refresh Tokens
top_articles.summary: Google OAuth Platform now supports DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) to sender-constrain refresh tokens, neutralizing Infostealer malware and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. By cryptographically binding long-lived refresh tokens while maintaining short-lived access tokens as standard Bearer tokens, developers achieve robust credential security without incurring high-QPS API performance overhead. Additionally, developers integrating multi-agent or Model Context Protocol (MCP) workloads can use Google Cloud Secure Token Service (STS) to handle secure token delegation across agent chains.

top_articles.title: Colab is now part of your Google AI plan
top_articles.summary: Unlock premium Google Colab compute with Google AI. Subscribers now get priority accelerators, Premium GPUs, and background execution for long training runs.

top_articles.title: The Outer Loop, Insights First: An Ambient Quality Agent That Diagnoses Your Production Agent
top_articles.summary: How do you keep improving an AI agent after the first 80%, once it serves real production traffic and silent quality regressions return HTTP 200 OK? We are open-sourcing AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent), a reference implementation that runs beside your production agent in Google Cloud, sweeps and verifies failure clusters against conversation transcripts, and diagnoses root causes anchored to the exact deployed source snapshot.

top_articles.title: Build zero-trust AI agents that judge intent, not just syntax
top_articles.summary: This blog post explores how to transition AI agents from static, build-time security controls to dynamic runtime governance using the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It highlights three primary managed defenses: Model Armor for screening edge prompts, Semantic Governance Policies for evaluating tool intent against business rules, and Agent Anomaly Detection for catching multi-turn exploits. By shifting these capabilities to the platform level, security administrators can dynamically enforce policies and neutralize complex attacks without needing to modify or redeploy the agent's underlying code.

top_articles.title: Evaluating AI agents: moving past the vibe check
top_articles.summary: A practical engineering guide and reference architecture for establishing continuous evaluation pipelines for multi-turn AI agents using Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Google ADK, and OpenInference standards.

top_articles.title: Reproducing Olmo 3 7B Pre-training in MaxText: case study of large scale training on TPUs
top_articles.summary: The MaxText team successfully reproduced Ai2’s Olmo 3 7B language model from scratch on Google Cloud TPUs using JAX/XLA, precisely matching the original PyTorch-on-GPU reference across pre-training and mid-training stages on all held-out evaluations. The implementation achieved up to 57.4% Model Flops Utilization (MFU) and demonstrated robust infrastructure portability by surviving mid-run cluster resizes and cross-generation TPU shifts without requiring recipe alterations. Crucially, the exercise proved the necessity of comprehensive held-out validation by catching a silent data-loader memorization bug that artificially depressed training loss and would have otherwise faked a performance win.

top_articles.title: Bring multimodal semantic search to the edge with EmbeddingGemma 2
top_articles.summary: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a new 740M open-weight multimodal model that maps text, images, video, and audio into a unified vector space for privacy-first, on-device retrieval. Developers can easily integrate these capabilities cross-platform using MediaPipe Tasks or optimize fine-grained performance across CPU, GPU, and NPU accelerators with LiteRT. The model enables ultra-low-latency local solutions like search-as-you-type media retrieval, keyframe video moments finding, and zero-shot intent routing.

DevOps.title: Why OpenGCUA Is the Secret Weapon That Could Slash Your Enterprise AI‑Ops Bill by 80%
DevOps.summary:
OpenGCUA’s “Fully Open Stack” Throws an Open‑Source Wrench Into the Computer‑Use‑Agent Market

Open‑source automation could slash enterprise AI‑ops costs by up to 80 %—and it arrives this week.

Subtitle: A free, inspectable alternative to proprietary agents promises to reshape how companies automate GUIs, CLIs and vision‑driven tasks.

Lead – 15 Oct 2026

On 15 Oct 2026 the arXiv pre‑print 2610.22200 unveiled OpenGCUA, a fully open stack for general‑purpose computer‑use agents. Within 24 hours the repository earned 280 up‑votes on Hugging Face and was forked hundreds of times. The announcement matters because enterprises currently spend billions on closed agents that charge per‑action fees for GUI clicks, CLI commands and vision tasks. OpenGCUA offers the same capabilities without a pay‑per‑action bill and with complete source‑code transparency, challenging the business models behind GPT‑6 Astra, Microsoft Copilot for Windows and other proprietary stacks.

Quick‑Start Example: One Script, Three Platforms

A data‑science team needs to pull a daily sales report from a Windows‑only ERP, clean the CSV on a Linux server, and load the result into Snowflake. With OpenGCUA a single agent script replaces three separate RPA tools:

Step What the agent does
Observe Uses Microsoft UIAutomation to click the ERP’s “Export” button and captures the dialog.
Act Sends the CSV through a CLI bridge that spawns a PTY on a Linux node, runs a Python transformer, and writes the cleaned file to a shared volume.
Authorize Requests a one‑click token from the team’s Slack‑integrated policy engine before uploading.
Complete Calls a Wasm‑based Snowflake plugin to push the payload; every action is logged via OpenTelemetry.

Result: One OpenGCUA process eliminates three licenses, three maintenance contracts and three failure points, saving the team ≈ $12 k per quarter in API fees and providing a single source of truth for debugging.

Hard Numbers & Release Cadence

Release Roadmap

  • Day 0–30: Core runtime, model‑API, sandbox released on GitHub.
  • Day 31–90: Vision pipeline and programmatic‑action library added.
  • Day 91–150: Safety layer (initiation‑authorization) shipped.
  • Q1 2027: Full Wasm‑based plugin marketplace opens.

The staggered cadence keeps the community engaged while giving enterprises a predictable path to production.

Technical Stack at a Glance

Economic Ripple

  • Per‑action fees eliminated. Proprietary agents charge $0.001–$0.005 per action; a mid‑size enterprise running 10 k actions monthly could spend $120 k–$600 k annually. OpenGCUA’s free core reduces that to zero, leaving only optional support or marketplace purchases.
  • Vendor lock‑in reduced. Companies can host the stack on‑premise, on any public cloud, or on edge devices, keeping data in‑house and easing GDPR, HIPAA and other compliance burdens.
  • New revenue streams. The Wasm marketplace enables developers to sell premium plugins (e.g., Salesforce automation, custom OCR). Early forecasts suggest a $2 M–$5 M annual market for third‑party extensions by 2029.

Competitive Positioning

Safety Token‑based initiation, auditable OpenTelemetry logs Provider‑side guardrails, opaque Microsoft‑managed policy engine, limited user control
Extensibility Wasm plugins, community marketplace Limited to OpenAI‑provided plugins Limited to Microsoft Graph extensions

OpenGCUA’s transparency and model‑agnostic design give it a clear edge for organizations that need reproducibility, cost predictability and regulatory compliance. The incumbents still benefit from massive cloud infrastructure, integrated productivity suites and brand trust, which will temper OpenGCUA’s immediate impact.

Top Three Risks & Mitigations

  1. Safety‑layer maturity – Manual token approvals can bottleneck high‑throughput pipelines.

    Mitigation: Deploy policy‑engine automation (e.g., rule‑based token issuance) and integrate with existing CI/CD approval workflows.

  2. Performance gap – The default Llama 3‑Open 8B trails GPT‑6 Astra on few‑shot reasoning and multimodal grounding.

    Mitigation: Encourage the community to fine‑tune open models on domain‑specific data; offer benchmark‑driven model‑selection guidance in the documentation.

  3. Marketplace chicken‑and‑egg – A limited plugin ecosystem may deter early adopters.

    Mitigation: Seed the marketplace with core integrations (Office, Salesforce, ServiceNow) funded by strategic partners; provide revenue‑share incentives for early plugin developers.

Outlook

  • 2026‑27: Pilot projects will appear in AI research labs (Stanford, DeepMind) and forward‑looking cloud providers experimenting with “open stacks for AI.” The Wasm marketplace will launch a beta with 30+ plugins focused on low‑friction integrations (Slack bots, file‑transfer utilities).
  • 2027‑28: As the plugin ecosystem matures, mid‑size enterprises will adopt OpenGCUA for internal automation, especially where data‑sovereignty rules prohibit external APIs. Analyst firms project a 10‑15 % shift of the computer‑use‑agent market toward open stacks, chipping away at the current 80 % dominance of closed solutions.
  • 2029 +: If the community delivers an open‑weight LLM that matches GPT‑6 Astra on benchmark performance, the cost advantage becomes decisive. A thriving marketplace could attract venture capital and lead to a commercial “OpenGCUA Enterprise” offering with SLA‑level support.

In the short term, OpenGCUA’s greatest asset is transparency. Companies that cannot afford opaque per‑action fees—and that must prove compliance to auditors—will begin with low‑risk pilot deployments. Successful pilots will generate real‑world benchmarks, pressure proprietary vendors to open parts of their APIs, and accelerate the shift toward generalist, inspectable computer‑use agents.

Bottom Line

OpenGCUA’s launch is a watershed moment for the computer‑use‑agent market. By delivering a fully open, modular stack that runs on every major OS and hardware platform, it forces incumbents to justify their closed, pay‑per‑action models. The rolling release schedule, Rust‑level performance and Wasm‑based extensibility give it a solid technical foundation. Yet the stack must overcome safety‑workflow friction, performance gaps and ecosystem bootstrapping challenges before it can claim a substantial market share.

If the community closes those gaps, the next few years could see a pluralistic market where enterprises choose the stack—open or closed—that best aligns with cost, compliance and capability, rather than being locked into a single vendor’s ecosystem. OpenGCUA may not rewrite the rulebook overnight, but it certainly hands the rulebook back to the developers.

Frontend.title: 74% of Indie Stores Are Invisible to ChatGPT Shopping. I Built an Open-Source Linter to Fix It (Gemma 2 + SerpApi)
Frontend.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

Here is a quiet shift happening in e-commerce right now: buyers are stopping at ten blue links and asking ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, and Gemini directly:

"Find me breathable eucalyptus running shoes in US 10.5 under $120 in stock right now."

When an AI shopping agent crawls a big brand like Nike or Amazon, it reads pristine, server-rendered Schema.org JSON-LD microdata.

When that same AI agent crawls an independent Shopify store or D2C side hustle, it frequently hits a brick wall:

  1. Silent Variant Dropouts: Client-side JavaScript size/color pickers hide secondary SKUs from non-browser crawlers. The store has Size 10.5 in stock, but the root HTML only exposes Size 8.
  2. Missing Global Identifiers: Missing GTIN/UPC barcodes prevent AI agents from cross-verifying product authenticity across merchant registries.
  3. Price & Catalog Drift: Secondary reseller sites (Poshmark, eBay, Depop) outrank the official merchant on Google Shopping with outdated or undercut pricing.

Enterprise brands pay $2,000+/month for catalog observability platforms to catch these issues. Indie merchants and solo founders can't afford that.

So I built CatalogPulse — a fast, zero-install, open-source AI Commerce Linter that lets any merchant, freelancer, or agency audit a product URL in 10 seconds, cross-reference live market listings via SerpApi Google Shopping, and generate a validated, copy-pasteable Schema.org Product JSON-LD fix powered by Google Gemma 2.

Frontend.title: PlxNative: A Fast Native Plex Client for LG webOS TVs, Built in Rust
Frontend.summary:
Most smart-TV apps are web pages. On LG's webOS that usually means JavaScript running inside a browser engine, which then hands its output to a compositor before anything reaches the screen. PlxNative is a Plex client for LG webOS TVs that takes that layer out. Its developer, Gleb Linnik, writes in the README: "No Chromium, no JavaScript, no web view. It just draws."

This is an explainer, built from the project's README, its docs, its source and its release notes. I don't own an LG TV, so nothing here was tested on a real television. What I did run is the project's own Linux desktop simulator against its mock Plex server, and that section near the end shows exactly what that does and doesn't tell you.

What PlxNative is

  • An unofficial Plex client for LG webOS TVs. It is not made by or affiliated with Plex or LG; the project says so on its site and in TRADEMARKS.md.
  • Open source under GPL-3.0-or-later, © 2026 Gleb Linnik. The PlxNative name and brand artwork are excluded from the licence.
  • One person's project. The README calls it "one person's spare time".
  • Current release: v0.8.0, published on GitHub on 7 October 2026. Nightly builds already report 0.9.0-nightly.
  • Young and active. The repository was created on 3 July 2026, and when I checked on 16 October it had 969 stars and 95 forks, with commits landing the same morning.
  • Free. There's no paid tier. You need a Plex account and a Plex Media Server, and the FAQ confirms a free Plex server works.

Why it exists

The origin story is short. The developer's 2019 LG TV still had a great picture, but browsing a Plex library on it "felt slower than it needed to." Rather than tune a web app, he wrote a native one. In his words: "I use it every day to watch things off my server in the next room."

The site makes the argument with a pair of stacks. A typical TV app goes:

The app (a web page) -> JavaScript -> Browser engine -> Compositor -> OpenGL -> GPU -> Screen

PlxNative goes:

The app (native code) -> OpenGL -> GPU -> Screen

The claimed result is 60 fps on that 2019 set. I couldn't measure that, and the project itself says the simulator can't either. More on that below.

The architecture

Mostly Rust, with a thin C shell

The repository is overwhelmingly Rust. A rough line count on the current main gives about 576,000 lines of .rs files against about 7,300 lines of C and C++. That count includes tests and generated data, so treat it as a ratio, not a measure of features.

The structure is spelled out in rust-modules/Cargo.toml. It's a Cargo workspace whose root crate is linked into a small C app as a static library:

# Static library linked into the C app (hybrid migration): each ported module
# exposes the same C ABI its src/*.h declares, so the C code calls it unchanged.
[lib]
name = "plxnative_modules"

The workspace is split into layer crates: base, machine, net, platform, gfx, ui, plex, telemetry, data, session, media, appkit, screens and storage. docs/module-layers.md describes how they depend on one another.

A GPU-drawn interface

The UI goes through SDL2 and OpenGL ES (both are listed in the repo's topics), so there's no DOM and no layout engine. The design language is translucent "glass" panels over your own posters and backdrops, with text sized for reading across a room. The docs folder holds design notes on liquid glass, backdrop blur and a hardware budget for the glass effect, which gives a sense of how much of the work goes into making that look cheap enough for TV silicon.

Video on the TV's own decoder

Playback doesn't decode video in software. The README says the app "hands video to the same silicon the built-in apps use". In the code, that goes through a video-sink trait in the platform crate. On the TV it's implemented by a StarfishSink, which talks to LG's Starfish media APIs, and on the desktop by a HostSink.

What it can direct-play, per the README:

  • H.264 and HEVC, including 4K and 10-bit
  • Dolby Vision profiles 5 and 8
  • E-AC-3 with Atmos
  • AV1 or VP9 (10-bit VP9 only on webOS 4 sets), on TVs whose codec table lists that decoder

Anything else is transcoded by your Plex server. Before you press Play, the detail page shows whether a title will play directly or be converted on the server. The app also ships its own LGPL build of FFmpeg.

Features

From the README, the site and the 0.8.0 release notes:

  • Sign in on the TV by scanning a QR code with your phone, then pick a Plex Home profile. PIN-protected profiles are supported.
  • Browse your own and shared libraries, with Continue Watching, Recently Added, sort, filters (including unwatched-only) and an A–Z rail.
  • Search across every server you can reach, with results grouped by kind.
  • A full player with resume, seek and scrub, chapters, audio and subtitle tracks (image subtitles included), Skip Intro, Skip Credits, Up Next with auto-advance, and progress synced back to Plex.
  • New in 0.8.0: subtitle search from inside the player, ASS/SSA subtitles that keep their styling, browsing Plex collections, Boost dialog and Normalize loudness on servers with Plex Pass, a Settings section for playback, and Spanish and Belarusian translations.
  • Works without internet after the first sign-in. The app talks to your server directly, so the library keeps working on your home network when the internet is down.
  • Privacy defaults. Crash reports and usage analytics are two separate opt-in questions, both off until you say yes. The README says no title, search term, subtitle line, server name or address can appear in any report. The app talks to your Plex server, to plex.tv to sign in, and to discover.provider.plex.tv for cast biographies.

0.8.0 also changes one security behaviour. Some home servers only answer over plain HTTP. Earlier versions refused to send your Plex sign-in that way. 0.8.0 will connect, but only after asking "Connect without encryption?", and only for a server on the same network at a private address after every secure route, Plex's relay included, has failed.

How to install it

PlxNative isn't in the LG Content Store yet; the site says it's "in the process of review" with no confirmed date. There are two routes, and neither needs root.

Route 1: LG Developer Mode

The installation guide needs an LG TV on webOS 4.0 or newer, a Plex account with a server, and a Mac, Windows or Linux computer on the same network. In short:

  1. Create or sign in to an account on LG's developer site.
  2. Install the Developer Mode app on the TV, sign in, turn on Dev Mode Status (the TV restarts) and then Key Server.
  3. Note the TV's IP address and passphrase, and connect to it from webOS Dev Manager on your computer.
  4. Install the .ipk directly, or install Homebrew Channel first and get PlxNative from its catalogue.

For a manual download, verify the package first:

sha256sum -c ipk.sha256

The catch is renewal. Developer Mode sessions expire, and if one lapses LG removes the apps installed through it. The guide's advice is to open the Developer Mode app and press EXTEND before the remaining time runs out, with a calendar reminder. An expired session can't be extended.

Route 2: Homebrew Channel

If your TV already runs Homebrew Channel, open it, find PlxNative (a 19.6 MB download, listed as version 0.8.0) and select Install. Updates arrive there too, and the Channel checks the download's checksum before installing.

Nightlies

Adding https://plxnative.com/nightly/repo.json to Homebrew Channel installs PlxNative Nightly as a separate app with its own tile and sign-in. The README is blunt about these builds: "It is not tested on a television."

Limits and current status

The README has a section titled "The honest scope", and it's worth taking at its word:

  • Movies and TV shows only. No music, no photos, no Live TV or DVR.
  • No typing in server addresses. Servers come from your Plex account.
  • Relay and secure-only servers are supported but "haven't been watched end to end."
  • Not all TVs work. It needs webOS 4.0 or newer. A 2016 set on webOS 3.4.3 has been tested and works.

The known issues list is specific:

  • Some 2019 sets on LG's k5lp or k3lp chip, installed through Developer Mode, won't play video. The sandbox withholds a device the video path needs; Kodi and Moonlight hit the same wall. Without root there's no fix.
  • 2018 sets on webOS 3.9.3: sign-in and browsing work, but the prebuilt v0.8.0 never starts video (#249). A source build at or after commit 60f99c7 fixes it.
  • webOS 3.x restarts the stream on every seek instead of jumping in place.
  • Sets on the k6hp chip show a crash in opt-in reports that the developer can't reproduce without the hardware (#174).

Building the simulator on Linux

Since I couldn't put it on a TV, I built the desktop simulator the docs describe. The box runs Debian 13 on x86_64 with 8 vCPUs and no GPU. The only prerequisites were the SDL2, SDL2_ttf, Mesa, CMake and pkg-config dev packages plus a current stable Rust toolchain:

git clone https://github.com/GLinnik21/plx-native && cd plx-native
make sim-linux SIM_TDIR=rust-modules/target-sim

   Compiling plxnative-modules v0.8.0 (/workspace/plxnative/repo/rust-modules)
    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 3m 08s
real    3m57.100s

That gave a 16 MB plxnative-sim binary on the first try. The extra 49 seconds went into fetching and building the libass stack (FreeType, FriBidi, HarfBuzz and friends).

The project's screenshot tool then boots the simulator against tests/mock_pms.py. That's a synthetic Plex server that also stands in for plex.tv, so no account, token or real library is involved. I ran it headless under Xvfb with software OpenGL:

python3 tools/demo_library.py derive
LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 xvfb-run -a -s '-screen 0 1920x1080x24' \
  python3 tools/screenshots.py --bin rust-modules/target-sim/release/plxnative-sim \
  --out shots --only home-shelves,library-grid,search,detail,signin

Each scene settled in 2.2 to 4.9 seconds. One hiccup: the home scene also renders the website's link-preview card, and that step failed because the box lacked the file utility, so I captured home-shelves instead.

The sign-in screen is the QR flow, here pointed at the mock:

The Movies grid, with the sort and filter chips and the A–Z rail, browsing the project's demo library of openly licensed films:

And a title page, with the "Direct Play" label next to the runtime:

Be clear about what this proves. The simulator runs the same UI and Plex code as the TV build, and it boots, signs in to a fake server and draws every screen I asked for. But docs/building.md says plainly that it "cannot answer frame rate (different GPU), text rasterization, or anything about LG's decoder and video plane. Those need the set." The Linux build also has no video path at all; the Makefile notes that Play "intentionally reaches the host seam's existing 'no video path' result." So the speed and the hardware decoding, the two things PlxNative exists for, are still unverified by me.

Who it's for

If you run Plex at home and own a fairly recent LG TV, PlxNative is a well-documented alternative to the official app. Expect a project that tells you about its rough edges in the README. You'll need to be comfortable with Developer Mode renewals or Homebrew Channel until the LG Content Store listing lands. If you need music, Live TV or a set from the known-issues list, the README itself says the official app will serve you better.

If you're a developer, the repository is interesting on its own terms: a Rust UI stack drawing straight to GPU on TV-grade hardware, with design and performance notes for almost every decision. The simulator builds in a few minutes on plain Linux if you want to look around.

  • Source: https://github.com/GLinnik21/plx-native

Frontend.title: How to Get Your Public IP Address From the Command Line
Frontend.summary:
The quickest way to get your public IP address from a terminal is curl https://ipcomet.com. It prints your address and nothing else, so the output can go straight into a script. This guide shows the same one-liner on macOS, Linux and Windows, how to do it from Python and Node.js, how to get your location and ISP as JSON, and how to choose between IPv4 and IPv6.

The one-line answer 

curl https://ipcomet.com

The output is a single line such as 203.0.113.7. The home page recognises command-line clients (curl, wget, PowerShell and similar) by their User-Agent and returns just the address instead of the web page. In scripts, use the explicit endpoint https://ipcomet.com/api/ip, which always returns plain text.

macOS and Linux 

curl https://ipcomet.com/api/ip
wget -qO- https://ipcomet.com/api/ip

macOS includes curl but not wget. To keep the result in a shell variable, use MYIP=$(curl -s https://ipcomet.com/api/ip). The -s flag hides curl's progress meter.

Windows

Windows 10 and 11 ship with curl, so curl.exe https://ipcomet.com/api/ip works in both Command Prompt and PowerShell. Type curl.exe rather than curl in PowerShell, where curl can be an alias for Invoke-WebRequest. The native PowerShell way is:

(Invoke-RestMethod https://ipcomet.com/api/ip).Trim()

Python

With the requests library:

import requests
print(requests.get("https://ipcomet.com/api/ip", timeout=10).text.strip())

With only the standard library, set a User-Agent. Python's default one (Python-urllib) is rejected by the bot protection in front of many sites, ipcomet included, which answer with a 403 error (Cloudflare error 1010):

import urllib.request

req = urllib.request.Request("https://ipcomet.com/api/ip", headers={"User-Agent": "my-script/1.0"})
print(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10).read().decode().strip())

JavaScript and Node.js 

const ip = (await (await fetch("https://ipcomet.com/api/ip")).text()).trim();
console.log(ip);

This works in Node.js 18 and later, which has fetch built in, and in a browser page, because the endpoint allows cross-origin requests.

Get your location and ISP as JSON 

curl https://ipcomet.com/api/me

The response describes the connection that made the request. An example, with made-up values:

{
  "ip": "203.0.113.7",
  "version": 4,
  "city": "Mumbai",
  "region": "Maharashtra",
  "country": "India",
  "countryCode": "IN",
  "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata",
  "asn": 64500,
  "org": "Example Broadband Ltd"
}

The full response also has the postal code, latitude and longitude, and a few details about the connection (the edge location, the HTTP and TLS versions and the round-trip time). To pick out one field, pipe it through jq: curl -s https://ipcomet.com/api/me | jq -r .country.

To look up any other address, use curl "https://ipcomet.com/api/lookup?q=8.8.8.8". It returns the IP version, hostname, city, region, country, coordinates, timezone, ASN and network owner. Lookups are limited to 60 a minute per caller, and location data is approximate because it comes from network records, not GPS.

Force IPv4 or IPv6

If your connection has both, add -4 or -6 to curl: curl -4 https://ipcomet.com forces IPv4, and curl -6 https://ipcomet.com forces IPv6, which only works if your connection has IPv6.

Other services you will see recommended

  • curl ifconfig.me, curl icanhazip.com, curl api.ipify.org and curl ipinfo.io/ip are other free services that return a bare address in the same way.
  • Without HTTP, you can ask a DNS resolver instead: dig +short myip.opendns.com @resolver1.opendns.com.

They all report the address the internet sees, so they should agree.

Why do two services show different IP addresses?

If they differ, your router may be sharing traffic across two internet connections, or a VPN may be carrying only some of your traffic.

These commands return your public address, the one websites see. For the private address on your own network, such as 192.168.1.20, check your network settings or run ipconfig on Windows and ip addr on Linux.

Limits and privacy

No key or sign-up is needed. Please keep requests reasonable: checking every few minutes is fine, but calling it in a tight loop may be rate limited. ipcomet does not store or log the addresses it sees. The free IP API page lists every endpoint with its exact rate limit.

This guide first appeared on ipcomet, a free IP checker I maintain.

Backend.title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Stream Ended at [DONE] and the File Was Still Half a Function
Backend.summary:
The transport told me the response was finished, and I believed it for about six hours. My collector had exited cleanly, the ledger showed [DONE], and the artifact on disk ended mid-expression inside a perfectly ordinary function body. Nothing raised, nothing logged, and the only reason I caught it was a linter run I almost skipped.

That is the failure mode I keep hitting when the model is free and the box is free: nothing is broken enough to page you. Over two days I rebuilt my collection loop around a simple rule — a stream is not a message, and only the message can be verified. This is what I tried, what broke, and what I would repeat on the next long job.

Why free access changes the shape of the bug

When inference costs real money per token, you naturally keep outputs short and your retry budget tight. Free model access plus a free server option inverts that incentive: long generations feel affordable, so you ask for whole modules, and you run the client somewhere you are not watching. Availability is the part I was given; latency, quotas, and durability are the part I refuse to assume.

So the interesting question is not "is the model good enough?" — it is "what does a truncated answer look like from the outside?" A dropped read timeout, a proxy that closes an idle connection, or a sleeping laptop all produce the same artifact: a prefix. And a prefix of valid code is often still valid code, which is exactly why it survives your smoke test.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Three files and one rule

My rule is boring: never append to a file you cannot describe. The collector keeps three artifacts in one directory, and each one answers a different question.

  1. answer.part — the raw bytes received so far, fsynced after every chunk.
  2. ledger.jsonl — append-only events: chunk offsets, prefix hashes, stream errors, verification verdicts.
  3. prompt.txt — the exact request text, written once before the first byte arrives.

Why the prefix hash and not just a byte count? Because a byte count tells you how much you have, while a hash tells you whether the thing you are about to continue is the thing you actually collected. If a resume writes into a different file than the one you hashed, you will not notice until the diff is unreadable.

The collector, labelled honestly

The script below is the version I would keep. Treat it as a lab artifact: it is unverified as written against your endpoint, so read it before you run it, and fill in the environment variables yourself.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""stream_ledger.py - collect a long completion with a resumable, verifiable ledger."""
import hashlib, json, os, pathlib, time
import requests  # pip install requests

BASE  = os.environ["MC_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")   # OpenAI-compatible base URL
KEY   = os.environ["MC_API_KEY"]
MODEL = os.environ.get("MC_MODEL", "your-model-id")
SENTINEL = "# ---END---"

WORK = pathlib.Path("run"); WORK.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
PART, LEDGER = WORK / "answer.part", WORK / "ledger.jsonl"


def note(event, **fields):
    rec = {"t": round(time.time(), 3), "event": event, **fields}
    with LEDGER.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(rec, sort_keys=True) + "\n"); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())


def append_chunk(text):
    with PART.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())
    return PART.stat().st_size


def prefix_sha():
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with PART.open("rb") as f:
        for block in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
            h.update(block)
    return h.hexdigest()


def stream(messages, read_timeout=90):
    with requests.post(f"{BASE}/chat/completions",
                       json={"model": MODEL, "messages": messages, "stream": True},
                       headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"},
                       stream=True, timeout=(10, read_timeout)) as r:
        r.raise_for_status()
        for line in r.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
            if not line or not line.startswith("data:"):
                continue
            data = line[5:].strip()
            if data == "[DONE]":
                note("transport_done", bytes=PART.stat().st_size, sha=prefix_sha()[:16])
                break
            try:
                piece = json.loads(data)["choices"][0]["delta"].get("content") or ""
            except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, IndexError):
                note("bad_frame"); continue   # one malformed frame is not a fatal error
            if piece:
                size = append_chunk(piece)
                note("chunk", bytes=size, sha=prefix_sha()[:16])
                yield piece

Two details matter more than the rest. The [DONE] frame is logged as transport_done, never as complete, because those are different claims. And a malformed frame skips instead of raising, since a single bad line should not cost you the whole generation.

The verifier that refuses a plausible prefix

The prompt ends with an instruction: finish the code, then emit the exact line # ---END--- on its own line. That sentinel is the whole trick, because it distinguishes "the model finished" from "the socket closed."

def verify(text):
    if not text.rstrip().endswith(SENTINEL):
        return False, "no sentinel: model output was cut, not completed"
    body = text.rsplit(SENTINEL, 1)[0]
    try:
        compile(body, "", "exec")
    except SyntaxError as e:
        return False, f"syntax error at line {e.lineno}: {e.msg}"
    return True, "parsed"

Notice the order. The sentinel check runs first, so a truncated but syntactically valid prefix fails fast instead of sailing through compile. If you only ever run the parser, you will ship half a function with a green checkmark.

Resuming without repeating the model to death

On failure I send back the last ~1200 characters as an assistant turn plus one short instruction: continue exactly there, no preamble, no summary. Two resumes maximum, then the run fails loudly. jq reads the ledger afterwards:

jq -r 'select(.event=="verify") | "\(.attempt)\t\(.ok)\t\(.why)"' run/ledger.jsonl

The 48-hour log

What broke, roughly in the order it broke.

  • Hour 2: I trusted [DONE]. Fix: a sentinel in the prompt, checked before anything else.
  • Hour 9: a resume duplicated the tail because I re-sent the full prompt without the partial answer. Fix: continuation messages always carry the tail as an assistant turn.
  • Hour 20: my verifier passed a file with balanced braces that ended inside a string literal. Fix: sentinel first, parser second, never the reverse.
  • Hour 31: I had two answer.part files and hashed the wrong one. Fix: the ledger records the absolute path next to every hash.
  • Hour 44: a long idle gap killed the connection and the retry loop ran four times silently. Fix: a resume cap of two, and a non-zero exit when it is hit.

What I would repeat without hesitation: one directory per run, fsync after every chunk, and a verdict line in the ledger for every attempt. The ledger is the only reason hour 31 was a ten-minute fix and not a rewrite.

Where this belongs, and where it does not

Workload Free model + free server? Guardrail
Long codegen you review before use Yes Sentinel, parser, two-resume cap
Batch docstring or test scaffolding Yes Same ledger, smaller outputs
Latency-sensitive request paths No No SLA to lean on
Regulated or secret data No You own the data-flow review, not the network
Anything you cannot re-run No Re-runnability is the whole safety net

Who should not use this? Anyone whose output feeds a deploy without a human read, anyone who cannot afford a second run, and anyone whose team will not look at ledger.jsonl when a job fails. If the ledger is noise to you, the workflow is just extra typing around a truncated file.

What I did not measure, and am not quoting

I am deliberately not publishing timings, throughput, or success rates here, because those numbers belong to your endpoint and your prompt shape, not to mine. The script prints its own offsets and verdicts, so your first run replaces every placeholder I could have invented. What I can say honestly is that the sentinel check caught truncations that compile() alone accepted, in more than one run.

If you already have free model access and a free server slot, the cheapest next step is small: point this collector at one long generation you already trust, and watch which hour your verify line flips to false after a transport_done.

FAQ

Is [DONE] ever a completion signal? It is a transport signal. The model's own end-of-output marker is the only thing that speaks for the content.

Do I need fsync on every chunk? It costs throughput and buys you a truthful file after a crash. For long codegen on a free box, I take the trade.

Can I skip the ledger if I only run once? You can, and then you will have no way to tell a truncated answer from a short one when it looks wrong.

Backend.title: Semantic Retrieval for E-commerce Product Search: Bounded Queries and Fresh Results
Backend.summary:
Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For an e-commerce catalog, that contract matters more than picking a fashionable embedding model: it keeps stale inventory and duplicate listings from becoming confident answers, and it leaves you a clean path to switch providers later.

I build RAG features with an eval harness beside the first notebook. The failure that shows up there is usually mundane. A product was re-indexed into a second collection, a tenant filter was dropped, or a web source timed out while the user waited. The fix is to make freshness and query limits part of the application contract, then measure each stage separately.

The retrieval contract comes before the vector store

Start by mapping the user-visible answer to fields you can inspect. Every indexed product needs a stable product or document identifier, tenant and access-control metadata, a source URL, and an ingestion timestamp. Keep those values attached to the chunk; do not reconstruct them from generated text after retrieval.

For a healthtech marketplace, that might mean a catalog PDF, a product monograph, and an access scope on every chunk. For a normal storefront, the same rule applies to SKU, locale, and seller. The domain changes; the contract does not.

Freshness is a policy, not a hope. Keep an active collection and a staging collection, write new chunks to staging, run duplicate and permission checks, and promote the collection only after the checks pass. A query then sees one well-defined snapshot instead of a race between old and new vectors.

Infrai fits at this boundary when you want to inspect a capability before binding your code to it. Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. Its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples, so a later ingestion or notification step does not create another credential ledger or a new SDK. That makes a trial easier to reverse because the contract stays in your code and the integration surface is plain HTTP.

That extra state is intentional. It makes a vendor migration reversible because your application depends on collection names and metadata semantics, not on a provider-specific index object. Measure twice.

How should semantic retrieval handle e-commerce product search query limits?

Bound every expensive step. Set a maximum candidate count for the vector query, a separate cap for reranking, and a wall-clock timeout for each source. If a source misses its deadline, return the best verified context you already have and record the miss for evaluation. Never let an unbounded web fetch decide whether the search page renders.

Keep it bounded.

The limit needs an owner. Put it in configuration, expose it in traces, and test the boundary with an empty result, exactly-full result, and an over-limit result. In a catalog refresh, a 40-item candidate cap might be fine for a broad category query but wasteful for an exact SKU lookup; the contract can choose different caps while preserving the same metadata and timeout guarantees. That is the kind of small, boring decision that keeps prompt cost from drifting when someone changes a default in a downstream service.

Here is the small piece I keep in a notebook before wiring a provider. It makes the limits explicit and keeps source context reviewable. The discovery request is public, so the example does not expose a key; production calls that read or write data use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY.

import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any

import requests


@dataclass
class RetrievalContract:
    collection: str
    max_candidates: int = 40
    max_rerank: int = 8
    timeout_seconds: float = 2.0


def discover_vector_capabilities() -> dict[str, Any]:
    key = os.environ.get("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"} if key else {}
    response = requests.get(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
        headers=headers,
        timeout=5,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()


def bounded_candidates(items: list[dict[str, Any]], contract: RetrievalContract):
    """Keep only reviewable results with source and access metadata."""
    accepted = []
    for item in items:
        if not item.get("source_url") or not item.get("document_id"):
            continue
        if not item.get("tenant_id") or not item.get("access_scope"):
            continue
        accepted.append(item)
        if len(accepted) == contract.max_candidates:
            break
    return accepted


def retry_after_429(call, attempts: int = 3):
    """Retry a rate-limited read with bounded exponential backoff."""
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        response = call()
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response
        delay = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        time.sleep(float(delay) if delay else 2**attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after bounded retries")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    key = os.environ.get("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    contract = RetrievalContract(collection="catalog-active")
    manifest = discover_vector_capabilities()
    print(manifest.get("version"), contract)
    print("Authenticated vector calls require INFRAI_API_KEY:", bool(key))

The code does not pretend that a generic top_k field is portable. Before adding an upsert or query call, read the request schema from the public discovery entry for that capability and map your contract fields explicitly. The useful property here is self-description: discovery exposes the capability schema and runnable examples, so adding a new backend means reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That shortens migration work without claiming that all stores behave identically.

What changes when freshness is measured instead of assumed?

I track four numbers in the eval harness: duplicate rate, stale-hit rate, permission-filter misses, and source-context completeness. Slice them by collection snapshot and query type. A single overall relevance score can look healthy while yesterday's price wins against today's inventory.

Run a freshness check after every ingestion batch. Sample products whose source timestamp changed, then assert that the active collection returns the newest permitted document. Also test a deleted listing: it should disappear from the active snapshot, not merely rank lower.

One early experiment taught me to separate retrieval from answer generation. I initially increased the candidate limit when results looked thin. That made prompts longer and did not fix duplicates; the real issue was two ingestion jobs writing the same SKU under different chunk IDs. A uniqueness check on (tenant_id, product_id, source_version) fixed the data contract, while the bounded query kept token use predictable.

Keep the logs useful but modest: query id, collection version, candidate count, timeout outcome, and source identifiers. Do not log raw protected document text by default. The trace should let a reviewer open the source URL or document identifier and understand why a result was eligible.

How do these options support a reversible product-search migration?

The right alternative depends on where you want the boundary. Elasticsearch gives teams mature lexical and filter tooling; Pinecone is a focused managed vector service; Weaviate combines vector search with a schema-oriented database experience. A provider with a broad REST surface can be attractive when search is one of several backend capabilities, provided your own contract remains in charge.

Option Strength for product search Migration trade-off
Elasticsearch Strong lexical search, filters, and operational familiarity More cluster and mapping decisions to carry between environments
Pinecone Focused managed vector indexes and namespaces Application code is coupled to its index/query model
Weaviate Schema plus vector features in one product Schema and module choices become part of your portability work
A self-describing REST layer One HTTP surface, with discovery and examples for capabilities You still own relevance tuning, snapshot policy, and provider-fit checks

For this workflow, I would try Infrai when the team wants that self-describing HTTP contract and expects to add adjacent capabilities without installing another SDK. Its discovery surface documents request and response schemas, and the platform uses one key across its broad capability set; that means the search worker, ingestion job, and a later notification step can share one credential and one integration pattern instead of accumulating separate client libraries and key-rotation paths. Those facts reduce integration inventory, while your collection and metadata contract preserves an exit route. I would stick with Elasticsearch when lexical relevance and deep faceting are the primary product, or choose Pinecone when a narrowly managed vector service is the requirement.

The catch is real: a unified API does not remove the need to validate ranking quality, filtering semantics, or regional data requirements. It is not suitable when your search team needs provider-specific indexing controls that the shared surface does not expose. Run the same golden-query set against at least two candidates before committing.

A reversible rollout plan

Put the retrieval contract behind a small Python interface. During migration, dual-write to staging only, compare IDs and source versions, and promote after the freshness and access-control checks pass. Keep the old collection readable until the new path meets the error and relevance thresholds in your eval harness.

Then remove the dual-write path in a separate change. That sequencing makes rollback a configuration decision instead of a weekend rewrite.

The measurement I would not skip is prompt cost. Candidate count, chunk size, and source citation fields all consume context. Your mileage may vary by catalog shape, and I'm not sure a single rerank limit will fit every language mix; record the distribution, not just the mean, before you tune it.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai discovery documentation and verify the live schema before implementing a write or query call.

  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/search/semantic-search
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/search/similarity

Backend.title: # From AI Prototype to Production: A Practical Guide to Deploying, Scaling, and Operating AI Systems
Backend.summary:
By Ahmed Adawy

Your AI application works on your machine. Your API returns responses. Your model integration looks promising. Your tests pass.

Then production introduces a different set of problems.

Dependencies behave differently across environments. Deployments become fragile. API latency increases under load. Secrets end up in the wrong place. Logs reveal too little when something breaks. A service that worked perfectly during development becomes difficult to monitor, secure, and maintain.

This is where AI engineering becomes production engineering.

Building an AI-powered application is only one part of the job. Operating it reliably requires a broader understanding of software architecture, deployment automation, infrastructure, observability, security, and performance.

That is the engineering problem behind my book:

The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate.

Read the book on Leanpub:
https://leanpub.com/theaiengineervolumeiideployscaleoperate

The Missing Step Between Building AI and Operating AI

Modern AI development makes it relatively easy to connect a Python application to an LLM, expose an API, generate embeddings, or build a semantic search pipeline.

But a working demonstration is not the same as a dependable production system.

Consider an AI document-processing service. Its basic workflow might look like this:

  1. Accept a document through an API.
  2. Validate the input.
  3. Extract and normalize the text.
  4. Generate embeddings or call an AI model.
  5. Store the results.
  6. Return a response to the client.

That workflow describes functionality, but it does not answer the operational questions.

What happens if the model provider times out? How does the application recover from a failed deployment? Where are credentials stored? How do you detect rising latency? Can the service handle concurrent requests? How do you prevent a database connection pool from becoming a bottleneck? How can you reproduce a production failure locally?

These are not secondary concerns. They determine whether an AI application can be operated reliably.

1. Docker: Make the Runtime Reproducible

An application depends on more than its source code. It also depends on a Python version, system libraries, installed packages, configuration, and runtime assumptions.

Docker helps package an application and its dependencies into a reproducible container image.

For a Python API built with FastAPI, a basic Dockerfile might look like this:

FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

This example assumes that requirements.txt exists and that the application exposes a FastAPI instance named app in app/main.py.

Build the image:

docker build -t ai-document-service .

Run the container:

docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 ai-document-service

The API should now be reachable at http://localhost:8000, assuming the application starts successfully.

This is a starting point, not a complete production security configuration. A production image should also consider a non-root user, dependency pinning, image scanning, secret management, and an appropriate build context.

The objective is to reduce environmental surprises and make the application easier to build, test, and deploy consistently.

2. CI/CD: Turn Deployment Into a Repeatable Process

Manual deployment creates opportunities for inconsistent steps, forgotten checks, and configuration mistakes.

A continuous integration and continuous delivery pipeline can automate the path from a code change to a deployable artifact.

A typical workflow looks like this:

Developer Push
      |
      v
Automated Tests
      |
      v
Static Checks
      |
      v
Build Container Image
      |
      v
Security and Artifact Checks
      |
      v
Deploy to Target Environment
      |
      v
Health Verification

The precise stages depend on the project, but the principle remains the same: make important deployment steps explicit and repeatable.

For an AI application, automated checks can cover request validation, authentication, document processing, database behavior, model-client error handling, and API contracts.

Not every test should call a live LLM. Many application tests can use deterministic fake clients to avoid unnecessary cost, network dependencies, and unpredictable model output.

A reliable pipeline should tell you not only that a deployment command completed, but also whether the deployed application is healthy enough to serve requests.

3. Cloud Deployment: Design for the Actual Runtime

Deploying an application to the cloud is not simply a matter of uploading code.

You need to understand the runtime environment, network access, configuration, storage, process management, health checks, and failure behavior.

An AI application might depend on:

  • A FastAPI service for HTTP requests.
  • A relational database for application records.
  • Object storage for uploaded documents.
  • An embedding service or vector database for semantic retrieval.
  • An external LLM provider.
  • Background workers for long-running tasks.

Each dependency creates an operational boundary.

If the model provider becomes slow, should the API wait indefinitely? If document ingestion takes several minutes, should it run inside the original HTTP request? If a deployment restarts the application, what happens to queued work?

These questions influence architecture before the first production incident occurs.

4. Kubernetes: Understand Orchestration Before Adding Complexity

Kubernetes provides mechanisms for deploying and managing containerized workloads, including scheduling, service discovery, health-based restarts, and scaling.

However, Kubernetes is not automatically the right choice for every AI application.

A small service may be easier and cheaper to operate on a managed application platform. A larger system with multiple services, more demanding availability requirements, and established infrastructure practices may benefit from orchestration.

The important engineering skill is understanding the trade-offs.

Before adopting Kubernetes, identify the operational problem you are solving. Then evaluate deployment complexity, resource requirements, observability, scaling behavior, team experience, and ongoing maintenance.

Infrastructure should serve the application rather than become an objective in itself.

5. Observability: Make Failures Investigable

When an AI application fails, a single message saying “Internal Server Error” rarely provides enough information to identify the cause.

Useful observability combines several sources of evidence:

Logs help explain what happened during a request.

Metrics reveal trends such as latency, request volume, error rates, memory consumption, and resource saturation.

Traces help follow a request across services and identify where time is being spent.

AI applications also benefit from measuring model-specific behavior, including provider latency, token usage, timeout frequency, retry counts, and retrieval performance.

For example, a slow response could originate from database access, embedding generation, a remote model call, or a queue that is falling behind. Without useful measurements, those possibilities are difficult to distinguish.

Operational logs must be designed carefully. Avoid recording API keys, access tokens, private documents, or unnecessary personal information. Diagnostic detail should improve investigation without exposing sensitive data.

6. Production Security: Protect the Entire AI Workflow

AI security is not limited to the model itself.

A production system may expose API endpoints, process untrusted files, store confidential information, communicate with external providers, and execute background jobs.

Security therefore needs to be considered across the complete application.

Important areas include:

  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Secret and credential management.
  • Input validation and request-size limits.
  • Dependency and container-image security.
  • Database permissions and secure connections.
  • Rate limiting and abuse prevention.
  • Safe handling of uploaded documents.
  • Appropriate retention and protection of sensitive data.
  • Monitoring for suspicious access and unexpected usage.

An application can produce correct AI outputs and still be insecure if its API exposes data, its credentials are mishandled, or its resource limits are poorly designed.

Security is an architectural responsibility, not a final checklist added just before launch.

7. Scaling and Performance: Measure Before Optimizing

Scaling an AI application involves more than adding servers.

Performance may be limited by database queries, connection pools, synchronous operations, network latency, large request payloads, embedding generation, model-provider limits, or inefficient background processing.

Different bottlenecks require different solutions.

Caching can reduce repeated work when the cached result remains valid. Background jobs can move long-running operations outside the request-response path. Database indexing can improve query performance. Batching may improve throughput when the underlying service supports it. Concurrency controls can help protect limited resources.

But every optimization introduces trade-offs.

Caching creates invalidation questions. Retries can amplify traffic during an outage. Larger batches can increase memory use and response latency. More workers can overwhelm a database or external API.

A sound performance process starts with measurements, identifies the actual bottleneck, applies a targeted change, and measures the result again.

8. Architecture and Production Readiness

A maintainable AI system separates responsibilities instead of placing every operation in one large request handler.

For example:

API Layer
    |
    v
Application Services
    |
    +---- Document Processing
    |
    +---- Embedding and Retrieval
    |
    +---- Model Integration
    |
    +---- Persistence
    |
    +---- Background Jobs
    |
    v
Infrastructure and External Services

The boundaries do not have to correspond to separate microservices. They can begin as modules inside a single application.

The goal is to make responsibilities clear, dependencies explicit, and important behavior testable.

A production-readiness review should ask whether the system can be deployed repeatedly, configured safely, monitored effectively, recovered after failure, and maintained without relying on undocumented manual steps.

What This Book Covers

The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate. focuses on the engineering practices that take AI applications beyond the prototype stage.

The book covers:

  • Docker and containerization.
  • Linux and production operations.
  • Git, GitHub, and engineering workflows.
  • Continuous integration and continuous deployment.
  • Cloud deployment and infrastructure.
  • Kubernetes and cloud-native operations.
  • Observability, logging, and monitoring.
  • Production security.
  • Scaling and performance engineering.
  • AI engineering architecture patterns.
  • Production-readiness reviews.
  • A final engineering challenge and reference materials.

The material is organized around the progression from deployment fundamentals to operating and evaluating a more complete production system.

This volume is intended for Python developers, backend engineers, AI engineers, and software developers who want to understand what happens after an AI application works locally.

It is also useful for engineers who want a more structured way to think about deployment decisions, operational failure modes, and the trade-offs involved in running real-world AI systems.

The Goal Is Not Just to Make It Work

A successful prototype proves that an idea can work.

A production system must also be deployable, observable, secure, recoverable, and maintainable.

That difference is where much of the real engineering begins.

If you are building AI applications and want to strengthen the engineering practices around deployment, infrastructure, monitoring, security, and scaling, explore the book here:

The AI Engineer — Volume II: Deploy. Scale. Operate.

https://leanpub.com/theaiengineervolumeiideployscaleoperate

Author: Ahmed Adawy

Build beyond the prototype. Understand the system. Operate it with confidence.

Topics

AI Engineering, Production AI, Python, FastAPI, Docker, CI/CD, Kubernetes, Cloud Deployment, MLOps, Observability, AI Infrastructure, Distributed Systems, Software Architecture, DevOps, Performance Engineering

Backend.title: My read-only Python scanner accidentally ran a Git helper
Backend.summary:
We were building a tool whose defining promise was simple: inspect unfamiliar repository configuration without executing its code. Then a test revealed that an ordinary-looking Git operation could launch a program defined by the repository itself.

A small assumption with big consequences

You're about to open a GitHub repository in your editor. You want to know which commands may run through package installation, trusted workspace tasks, devcontainer startup, MCP servers or an AI coding agent. A static auditor looks like a reasonable first line of review.

ClonePeek was designed for that job. Its scanner traverses recognized configuration files using bounded reads and reports trigger → command → source location → suggested review , without launching the project's npm scripts, shell hooks, or coding agents.

There is a useful optional flag: --changed-since filters findings to Git changes. Our first implementation called a local git diff command. It felt harmless. Diffing files isn't building the repository, right?

The catch is that Git's execution behavior can depend on checkout-local or inherited configuration, not just the arguments my code passes. In particular, a local core.fsmonitor setting can name a hook-like helper program. Depending on the command and Git version, Git may invoke that helper while refreshing file state. A subprocess invoked by the auditor was therefore enough to break our passive-scan invariant.

One important boundary: a normal git clone does not transfer the remote repo's .git/config. The issue is an existing checkout and its local configuration or inherited Git environment; don't confuse it with a malicious package.json remotely rewriting Git config simply by being cloned.

Making the regression observable

To test this safely, we created a disposable local fixture with a deliberately inert helper that merely wrote a marker file. We did not use a real suspicious repository, download an executable payload, or depend on a network request.

The test asked one specific question: can the audit complete without creating that marker? Before the fix, the marker appeared. After the fix, it did not. Reproducing the violation as a filesystem side effect made it much harder for later refactors to accidentally reintroduce it.

This is not a claim that every git diff invocation on every operating system will execute an fsmonitor helper. It's a concrete example of why "I only ran Git" doesn't establish that no repo-defined execution occurred.

The exact reproduction and safety constraints are in the Git configuration isolation notes; the patch and review trail are in PR #5.

The defense has to cover the helper process

Python's read-only filesystem operations were not the issue. The boundary changed when the scanner delegated work to Git, a separate executable capable of honoring configuration, helpers and extensions. Fixing it required controlling both process arguments and the environment.

# Excerpted structure, not a standalone security sandbox
argv = [
    "git",
    "-c", "core.fsmonitor=false",
    "-c", f"core.hooksPath={os.devnull}",
    "-c", "diff.external=",
    "-c", "protocol.ext.allow=never",
    "-c", "protocol.file.allow=never",
    "-C", str(repo_root),
    "diff", "--no-ext-diff", "--no-textconv",
    "--name-only", "-z", "--diff-filter=ACMR",
    reference, "--",
]

The scanner also strips inherited Git-specific variables and dangerous loader/Python environment overrides, disables system/global Git config for this invocation, rejects unexpected ref syntax, bounds subprocess runtime, and treats a failed diff as an error rather than silently reporting an empty result. These are defense-in-depth choices for an explicitly limited operation ; they are not equivalent to process isolation.

Important limit: This hardening is targeted to the Git invocation used by ClonePeek. Git and the host operating system have more behavior than one wrapper can model. Do not treat ClonePeek as a sandbox, a malware detector, or a reliable way to execute other tools against actively malicious content.

The next surprise was a script one file away

Another coverage gap turned out to be less dramatic but equally useful. A package.json file could contain a short lifecycle command such as sh ./scripts/setup.sh. A surface-only scanner recognized the install hook, but the interesting command might live inside scripts/setup.sh, outside the JSON.

We added bounded, first-hop, read-only inspection for statically identifiable local .sh references. It checks that paths stay inside the repository, rejects symlink escapes and unsafe file types, and limits references, file sizes and lines read. It doesn't shell-expand arbitrary expressions or chase unbounded nested scripts.

That sounds modest—and that's intentional. A scanner that executes the referenced script "to find out what it does" would solve one detection problem by discarding its own execution boundary. ClonePeek instead tells you what it can and can't see.

Testing a release from outside the repository

Internal tests can miss assumptions about packaging. The v0.5.0 GitHub Action therefore has separate integration CI on Linux, macOS and Windows, plus an actual consumer workflow in another repository. That consumer workflow read two pinned, public configuration snapshots (Cursor hooks and VS Code folder-open tasks), checked their Git blob hashes, and asserted paths and classifications. No upstream hooks were run.

These are narrow smoke tests, not independent outside-user adoption or an estimate of detection accuracy. The hand-authored synthetic evaluation deliberately includes false positives and false negatives; it is not representative of internet repositories.

A checklist for tools that inspect untrusted projects

  • Map all execution paths, including your own helper commands. A safe-looking wrapper doesn't make delegated subprocesses inert.
  • Write regression tests around side effects, not only output strings. A marker file can reveal unexpected execution even when the scanner report looks correct.
  • Constrain filesystem reads and traversal. Symlinks, special files, large files and path escapes matter even when you never execute a script.
  • Separate supported detection from safety claims. A command hook is a review prompt, not proof that an author is malicious.
  • Make failure visible. Parse errors and unsupported references should not silently become "nothing found."

If you're auditing a repository you don't trust, the safest workflow begins before installing its dependencies or marking it trusted in an IDE. The five-minute pre-trust audit guide covers practical next steps.

Try it. Critique it. Improve it.

ClonePeek v0.5.1 is MIT licensed, has no runtime Python dependencies, and exposes its threat model publicly. We're looking for real, inert examples of execution hooks it misses or overclassifies—not drive-by stars or artificial PRs.

uvx --from git+https://github.com/harshitethic/clonepeek@v0.5.1 \
  clonepeek /path/to/repository

Browse source ↗ Contribute a real improvement ↗ Live demo ↗

Disclosure: I maintain ClonePeek. This case study was prepared with AI writing assistance and reviewed against the source, tests, and public docs. Maintainer-run tests are not independent security evaluation.
